## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of 128-bit shifts, wrap-around logic, and edge cases where n==0. Requires a clean, branch-minimal implementation without loops.

## Key Concepts
- Bitwise rotation across 128 bits
- Handling edge cases safely (n==0, 128-n)
- Avoiding undefined shifts across boundary bits

## Code Example
```c
uint128 rotateLeft128(uint128 x, uint8 n) {
  n &= 127;
  if (n == 0) return x;
  return (x << n) | (x >> (128 - n));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt for a language without 128-bit integers?
- How would compiler optimizations affect this implementation in real code?

## Why This Is Asked

```javascript
function rotl32(n, k) {

  return ((n << k) | (n >>> (32 - k))) >>> 0;
}
```

## Why This Is Asked

This question tests understanding of parity computation and branchless reduction techniques—skills essential in cryptography (e.g., Hamming code validation, checksums) and error-detection routines where constant-time operations matter.

## Key Concepts

- **Parity**: The XOR of all bits; 1 if an odd number of 1s, 0 if even.
- **XOR folding**: Successive shift+XOR operations collapse bit ranges without branches or loops.
- **128-bit handling**: Splitting into hi/lo halves and recombining.

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you adapt `parity128` to a 256-bit type?
- What is the time and space complexity of this approach?
- How would you make this constant-time for security-sensitive applications?

## Why This Question Is Asked
Tests the ability to decompose a 128-bit integer into 32-bit lanes and recombine them in a different order without using branches.

## Key Concepts
- Representing a 128-bit integer as two 64-bit halves (hi and lo)
- Extracting 32-bit lanes using bit masks and shifts
- Reassembling via shifts and bitwise ORs

## Common Pitfalls
- Confusing the mapping between bits and lanes
- Forgetting to mask after right-shifting (to isolate the lower 32 bits)
- Incorrectly pairing the extracted lanes when reassembling
